title: 第 43 課｜作用量作為座標的函數｜Landau–Lifshitz 經典力學
description:
當初講最小作用量原理時，我們把作用量看成沿著一條路徑的積分，兩個端點的位置和時刻都是給定的；在所有這些路徑裡，真實運動走的那一條讓積分最小。現在換一個角度看作用量：固定起點不動，但讓終點跑到不同的位置去，於是作用量變成終點座標的函數，而且我們只沿著真實的運動路徑來算它。把作用量做變分，會得到兩部分：一個邊界項，加上一個積分。因為真實路徑滿足拉格朗日方程，那個積分恆等於零。起點固定，所以起點的變分是零，剩下的邊界項就是動量乘上終點的變分；對多個自由度也一樣，每個座標配上它自己的動量。由此得到一個漂亮的結論：作用量對座標的偏導數，就等於對應的動量。換句話說，動量是作用量的梯度。在位形空間裡畫出作用量的等值面，動量就處處垂直於它們——就像光學裡的波前與光線。同樣地，也可以讓終點的時刻變動：起點與終點的位置都固定，但抵達的時刻不同，這樣作用量又成了時間的函數。要算它對時間的偏導數，最簡單的辦法是這樣：按定義，沿著路徑走，作用量的全時間導數就等於拉格朗日量。另一方面，把作用量看成座標與時間的函數，全導數等於對時間的偏導數，加上對每個座標的偏導數乘上速度；而剛才已經知道那些偏導數就是動量。兩邊一比較，就得到作用量對時間的偏導數，等於拉格朗日量減去動量乘速度的總和——那正好是哈密頓量的負值。把兩個結果合起來，作用量的全微分就是動量乘座標的微分加總，再減去哈密頓量乘時間的微分。作用量因此成了一座橋：它對座標的梯度是動量，對時間的導數是負的能量，而下一步就是漢彌頓－雅可比方程。

本影片為《Landau–Lifshitz 經典力學》教學系列第 43 課（繁體中文版）。

title: Lesson 43 | The Action as a Function of the Coordinates | Landau–Lifshitz
description:
When we set up the principle of least action, the action was an integral along a path whose two endpoints were both fixed in position and in time, and among all those paths the true motion is the one that makes the integral least. Now look at the action differently: keep the starting point fixed but let the far end move to different places. The action then becomes a function of the final coordinates, evaluated always along the true path of the motion. Varying it produces two pieces, a boundary term and an integral, and because the true path satisfies Lagrange's equations that integral vanishes identically. The start is fixed, so its variation is zero, and the boundary term that survives is the momentum times the variation of the endpoint; with several degrees of freedom each coordinate carries its own momentum. That gives a beautiful result: the derivative of the action with respect to a coordinate is the corresponding momentum, so momentum is the gradient of the action. Draw the level surfaces of the action in configuration space and the momenta stand perpendicular to them, like wavefronts and rays in optics. In the same way we can let the arrival time vary: both endpoints fixed in place, but reached at different instants, which makes the action a function of the time as well. To find its partial derivative with respect to time, the shortest route is this: by the very definition of the action, its total time derivative along the path is just the Lagrangian. On the other hand, treating the action as a function of coordinates and time, the total derivative is the partial one plus the derivative with respect to each coordinate times the velocity, and we already know those derivatives are the momenta. Comparing the two expressions, the partial derivative of the action with respect to time equals the Lagrangian minus the sum of momentum times velocity, and that is precisely minus the Hamiltonian. Putting both results together, the total differential of the action is the sum of momentum times the coordinate differential, minus the Hamiltonian times the time differential. The action is therefore a bridge: its gradient is momentum, its time derivative is minus the energy, and the next step from here is the Hamilton-Jacobi equation.

Lesson 43 of the Landau–Lifshitz Classical Mechanics teaching series (English edition).
